label: Before 1600
title: This land already has many nations
summary: Long before French and British colonies, Indigenous peoples lived in diverse societies across these lands. They had languages, laws, governments, trade networks and relationships with the land. European voyages and coastal trade were under way in the 1500s; colonial claims did not make these lands empty.
watch: Begin with the land and water. Why might rivers, coasts and lakes matter for travel, trade and community?
grade4: Describe how a river or coast could connect communities. What does this map leave out about the people who lived here?
grade7: A political map depends on whose perspective it shows. What information would you need to represent Indigenous homelands, relationships and governments?
keyIdea: No French or British colonial colours are used in this context view. The modern coastline is a geographic reference; it is not a map of precise Indigenous boundaries.
mapNote: Geographic context · modern coastlines, no provincial borders. Indigenous territories and relationships are not drawn as fixed polygons.

title: French and English colonies compete
summary: French settlements grow along the St. Lawrence and in Acadia, while English colonies develop on the Atlantic coast. Fur trade routes and alliances connect European settlements with Indigenous nations. This Atlas map shows European claims and disputed areas, not the disappearance of Indigenous homelands.
watch: Find New France, Acadia and the English colonies. Compare these colours with 1713.
grade4: Locate New France and Acadia. Which waters connect these places?
grade7: Compare 1667 with 1713. Which claims change, and which areas are shown as disputed?
keyIdea: Colonial claims and settlement are different. A large coloured area does not mean European settlers occupied or governed every part of it.

markers.name: New France
markers.note: A French colonial claim extending through the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes region. Indigenous nations continued to live and govern throughout these lands.

markers.name: Acadia
markers.note: French and English powers contested Acadia. Its colonial boundaries changed and were disputed.

markers.name: English colonies
markers.note: English colonies developed along the Atlantic coast south of Acadia.

title: France gives up several colonial claims
summary: The Treaty of Utrecht shifts claims to Acadia, Newfoundland and the Hudson Bay region toward Britain. France retains Canada in New France and the Gulf islands, including Île Royale (Cape Breton) and Île Saint-Jean (Prince Edward Island). The limits of Acadia remain contested.
watch: Compare with 1667. Find Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and the Hudson Bay region. Where do French claims remain?
grade4: Name two areas whose colonial control changes. Find a place still associated with France.
grade7: Why could a treaty between European powers leave a boundary disputed? Whose agreement is missing from this map?
keyIdea: Parks Canada notes that the treaty was not recognized by First Nations and left boundaries unclear in Acadia. European agreements did not settle Indigenous rights.

markers.name: Nova Scotia / Acadia
markers.note: France cedes Acadia under the treaty. Britain and France interpret its limits differently, and First Nations do not recognize the transfer as settling their rights.

markers.name: Newfoundland
markers.note: France relinquishes interests in Newfoundland while retaining fishing rights. The island is shown with British colonial colours.

markers.name: Hudson Bay / Rupert’s Land
markers.note: The treaty recognizes British rights in Rupert’s Land and restores Hudson Bay forts. Stripes on the Atlas map show disputed claims.

markers.name: New France
markers.note: France retains its colony of Canada in New France. The blue colour represents a French claim.

markers.name: Île Royale and Île Saint-Jean
markers.note: France retains these Gulf islands: today’s Cape Breton Island and Prince Edward Island.

title: British control expands; Quebec is defined
summary: The Treaty of Paris ends the Seven Years’ War. France cedes Canada to Britain, while keeping Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. In October, the Royal Proclamation organizes the Province of Quebec around the St. Lawrence and sets rules for colonial settlement and Crown purchases of First Nations lands.
watch: Find the small Province of Quebec. Why is it smaller than the former French claims? Locate the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes.
grade4: What changes in colonial control? Explain one reason the Royal Proclamation matters to First Nations.
grade7: Separate the two events: what does the Treaty of Paris transfer, and what does the Royal Proclamation organize and protect?
keyIdea: The Royal Proclamation recognizes that First Nations lands cannot simply be taken or privately purchased by settlers. It establishes Crown procedures for land agreements and remains foundational to treaty relationships.

markers.name: Province of Quebec
markers.note: The Royal Proclamation creates a smaller Province of Quebec around the St. Lawrence. British control of former French territory is broader than this colony’s boundary.

markers.name: Lands outside the colony
markers.note: The old source labels some areas “Indian Country.” These are Indigenous lands, not empty land. The Royal Proclamation restricts settlement and private land purchases.

markers.name: Newfoundland and Labrador coast
markers.note: The Proclamation places the Labrador coast and nearby islands under Newfoundland’s administration.

markers.name: Nova Scotia and Gulf islands
markers.note: Cape Breton and Île Saint-Jean are attached to Nova Scotia at this stage.

markers.name: Saint-Pierre and Miquelon
markers.note: France retains these small islands near Newfoundland under the Treaty of Paris.

title: Quebec grows; French civil law is restored
summary: Passed in 1774 and effective in 1775, the Quebec Act expands the colony into the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley and adds Labrador and nearby islands. It restores French civil law for property and civil rights and protects the practice of Catholicism, while British criminal law remains.
watch: Compare Quebec in 1763 and 1774. Follow the expansion toward the Great Lakes and the Ohio Valley.
grade4: Describe how Quebec’s territory changes. How did the Act help Francophone people maintain important parts of their lives?
grade7: Connect geography and rights: how did the Act change the colony’s extent, legal system and religious protections?
keyIdea: Francophone rights involve more than a boundary. The Act restores French civil law and protects Catholic religious practice; continued French language use is supported implicitly, rather than through a modern language-rights clause.

markers.name: Expanded Quebec
markers.note: Quebec’s colonial boundary extends toward the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. First Nations continue to live in these lands; changing colonial jurisdiction does not erase their rights.

markers.name: Labrador and Gulf islands
markers.note: Labrador, Anticosti and the Îles de la Madeleine are attached to Quebec under the Act.

markers.name: Ohio Valley
markers.note: The expanded boundary reaches the Ohio Valley, south of the Great Lakes. This is outside present-day Canada.

markers.name: St. Lawrence communities
markers.note: The Act restores French civil law and protects Catholic practice for the colony’s largely Francophone population.

title: Quebec becomes Upper and Lower Canada
summary: The Constitutional Act divides the Province of Quebec into Upper Canada and Lower Canada, each with its own legislature. Upper Canada lies upstream along the Great Lakes; Lower Canada lies downstream along the St. Lawrence. These are British colonies, not the modern provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
watch: Find the Ottawa River and the St. Lawrence. “Upper” and “Lower” refer to the river system, not north and south.
grade4: Use the rivers to explain the names Upper Canada and Lower Canada.
grade7: Compare 1774 and 1791. What does the new internal boundary do, and why do these colonies differ from modern Ontario and Quebec?
keyIdea: By 1791, the 1783 peace settlement has also changed the boundary with the United States. Not every difference from the 1774 map was caused by the Constitutional Act.

markers.name: Upper Canada
markers.note: A British colony mainly upstream along the Great Lakes. Its historical extent differs from modern Ontario.

markers.name: Lower Canada
markers.note: A British colony mainly downstream along the St. Lawrence, with a Francophone majority. Its historical extent differs from modern Quebec.

markers.name: Ottawa River
markers.note: The division between Upper and Lower Canada follows the Ottawa River in this area.

markers.name: New Brunswick
markers.note: A separate British colony, created in 1784. It is not part of Upper or Lower Canada.

markers.name: United States
markers.note: The United States is separate from the British colonies after the 1783 peace settlement.

title: Two colonies become the Province of Canada
summary: The Act of Union passes in July 1840 and takes effect on February 10, 1841. It joins Upper Canada and Lower Canada into one Province of Canada with one legislature. Their two sections become known as Canada West and Canada East. Other British colonies remain separate.
watch: Find the Province of Canada, then identify Canada West and Canada East. One political union does not mean every British colony has joined.
grade4: Which two colonies are united? Which colonies shown on the reference map remain separate?
grade7: Explain the difference between this political union and Confederation in 1867. What does a boundary map tell us, and what can it not tell us about government?
keyIdea: The Act initially restricts French in the legislature’s official records; that restriction is repealed in 1848. A union on the map does not guarantee equal treatment.
mapNote: 1849 reference map: it shows the Province of Canada created in 1841, plus later changes including the 1846 Oregon Treaty and the 1849 Vancouver Island colony. It is not an exact 1841 snapshot.
sourceLabel: Atlas of Canada, 4th edition · 1849 reference map

markers.name: Province of Canada
markers.note: Upper and Lower Canada are united in 1841. The two sections, Canada West and Canada East, share one legislature.

markers.name: Canada West
markers.note: Former Upper Canada, now the western section of the Province of Canada.

markers.name: Canada East
markers.note: Former Lower Canada, now the eastern section of the Province of Canada.

markers.name: Separate Atlantic colonies
markers.note: New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland remain separate from the Province of Canada.

markers.name: Later western changes
markers.note: This reference map is dated 1849. It includes the Oregon Treaty boundary of 1846 and the Vancouver Island colony of 1849.

title: Four provinces form Canada
summary: On July 1, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia form the new Dominion of Canada. Ontario and Quebec are much smaller than they are today. The grey regions have not joined Canada.
watch: Find the four coloured provinces. How different is this from the Canada you know?
grade4: Find the four coloured provinces. How different is this from the Canada you know?
grade7: Find the four coloured provinces. How different is this from the Canada you know? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Manitoba and the Northwest Territories
summary: Rupert’s Land and the North-Western Territory are transferred to Canada. Most of this land becomes the Northwest Territories. Manitoba enters Confederation as a small province around the Red River, following negotiations led by the Métis provisional government.
watch: Look for the original Manitoba. Why is it sometimes called the “postage-stamp province”?
grade4: Look for the original Manitoba. Why is it sometimes called the “postage-stamp province”?
grade7: Look for the original Manitoba. Why is it sometimes called the “postage-stamp province”? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: British Columbia joins
summary: British Columbia becomes Canada’s sixth province. Its boundary is the one established for the united colony in 1866. Canada now reaches the Pacific coast.
watch: Find British Columbia. Is all the land between it and Ontario part of a province?
grade4: Find British Columbia. Is all the land between it and Ontario part of a province?
grade7: Find British Columbia. Is all the land between it and Ontario part of a province? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Prince Edward Island joins
summary: Prince Edward Island becomes the seventh province. The agreement includes Canada taking on the island’s railway debt, buying land from absentee landlords, and providing a connection with the mainland.
watch: Find the small island in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Use the region list if it is hard to click.
grade4: Find the small island in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Use the region list if it is hard to click.
grade7: Find the small island in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Use the region list if it is hard to click. What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Ontario’s provisional boundary grows
summary: The federal government sets provisional northern and western boundaries for Ontario. Ontario’s western boundary remains a source of disagreement with Manitoba.
watch: Compare Ontario with 1873. In which directions has its boundary moved?
grade4: Compare Ontario with 1873. In which directions has its boundary moved?
grade7: Compare Ontario with 1873. In which directions has its boundary moved? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: The District of Keewatin is created
summary: A portion of the Northwest Territories becomes the District of Keewatin. This separate federal district is intended to provide temporary administration for land north and east of Manitoba and west of Ontario.
watch: Find Keewatin. A district is an administrative area; it is not a new province.
grade4: Find Keewatin. A district is an administrative area; it is not a new province.
grade7: Find Keewatin. A district is an administrative area; it is not a new province. What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: The Arctic islands become part of Canada
summary: Britain transfers its remaining Arctic territories and islands to Canada. Newfoundland remains outside Confederation. The transferred islands become part of the Northwest Territories.
watch: Look north. Which large grey region has changed to a Canadian territory?
grade4: Look north. Which large grey region has changed to a Canadian territory?
grade7: Look north. Which large grey region has changed to a Canadian territory? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Manitoba expands
summary: Manitoba’s boundaries move west, north, and east. Ontario objects to the eastern extension, so the map marks a disputed area between the two provinces.
watch: Find the striped disputed area. How can a map show that a boundary is not agreed upon?
grade4: Find the striped disputed area. How can a map show that a boundary is not agreed upon?
grade7: Find the striped disputed area. How can a map show that a boundary is not agreed upon? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Four western districts are established
summary: Assiniboia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Athabasca become provisional districts within the Northwest Territories. These districts help administer the region as settlement and railway construction increase.
watch: Find the Alberta district. Does it have the same outline as the province today?
grade4: Find the Alberta district. Does it have the same outline as the province today?
grade7: Find the Alberta district. Does it have the same outline as the province today? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Keewatin’s boundary is adjusted
summary: The southwestern boundary of the District of Keewatin is adjusted to fit the boundaries of the western districts created in 1882.
watch: Turn on previous boundaries and look at Keewatin’s southwestern edge.
grade4: Turn on previous boundaries and look at Keewatin’s southwestern edge.
grade7: Turn on previous boundaries and look at Keewatin’s southwestern edge. What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Ontario and Manitoba’s dispute is settled
summary: The Ontario Boundary Act settles the Ontario–Manitoba boundary dispute. Ontario extends west to Lake of the Woods and north to the Albany River.
watch: Compare 1881 and 1889. What has happened to the striped area?
grade4: Compare 1881 and 1889. What has happened to the striped area?
grade7: Compare 1881 and 1889. What has happened to the striped area? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: The northern districts are reorganized
summary: Ungava, Mackenzie, Yukon, and Franklin are established as additional districts in the Northwest Territories. Athabasca and Keewatin are enlarged.
watch: Locate Yukon and Ungava. What are these areas called on a later map?
grade4: Locate Yukon and Ungava. What are these areas called on a later map?
grade7: Locate Yukon and Ungava. What are these areas called on a later map? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Northern district boundaries change
summary: The boundaries of Franklin, Keewatin, Mackenzie, Ungava, and Yukon districts are adjusted. These are changes to administrative districts rather than the creation of provinces.
watch: Use previous boundaries to compare the northern districts with 1895.
grade4: Use previous boundaries to compare the northern districts with 1895.
grade7: Use previous boundaries to compare the northern districts with 1895. What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Yukon becomes a separate territory
summary: Yukon is separated from the Northwest Territories to become Yukon Territory. Quebec’s northern boundary extends to the Eastmain River.
watch: Find Yukon Territory, then compare Quebec with the previous map.
grade4: Find Yukon Territory, then compare Quebec with the previous map.
grade7: Find Yukon Territory, then compare Quebec with the previous map. What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Yukon’s boundary is adjusted
summary: Yukon Territory’s boundaries are adjusted to the outline shown in later Atlas snapshots.
watch: Look closely at Yukon with previous boundaries switched on. Some changes are much smaller than others.
grade4: Look closely at Yukon with previous boundaries switched on. Some changes are much smaller than others.
grade7: Look closely at Yukon with previous boundaries switched on. Some changes are much smaller than others. What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Alberta and Saskatchewan become provinces
summary: Alberta and Saskatchewan are created from the Northwest Territories. Canada now has nine provinces. Keewatin is returned to the Northwest Territories and continues as one of its districts.
watch: Compare the new provinces with the earlier western districts. Which boundaries have disappeared?
grade4: Compare the new provinces with the earlier western districts. Which boundaries have disappeared?
grade7: Compare the new provinces with the earlier western districts. Which boundaries have disappeared? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Three provinces extend north
summary: Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec extend northward. Ungava becomes part of Quebec, and Keewatin loses much of its land. Offshore islands are not included in Quebec’s extension. The remaining northern districts belong to a single Northwest Territories.
watch: Look at the large Northwest Territories label. How do the smaller district labels show parts of one territory?
grade4: Compare these three provinces with 1905. Which reaches Hudson Strait?
grade7: Compare these three provinces with 1905. Which reaches Hudson Strait? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?
keyIdea: Mackenzie, Keewatin and Franklin are historical districts within one Northwest Territories. Their colours distinguish districts; they do not represent separate territories.

title: Northern district boundaries are defined
summary: The boundaries of districts within the Northwest Territories are formally redescribed. This records changes following the creation of Alberta and Saskatchewan and the northern extensions of Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec.
watch: Look at Mackenzie, Keewatin, and Franklin. These are districts within the Northwest Territories.
grade4: Look at Mackenzie, Keewatin, and Franklin. These are districts within the Northwest Territories.
grade7: Look at Mackenzie, Keewatin, and Franklin. These are districts within the Northwest Territories. What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?
keyIdea: Mackenzie, Keewatin and Franklin are historical districts within one Northwest Territories. Their colours distinguish districts; they do not represent separate territories.

title: The Labrador boundary is defined
summary: The British Privy Council defines the boundary between Canada and Newfoundland in Labrador. Newfoundland is still outside Confederation at this point. The Atlas shows the boundary established by this decision.
watch: Compare Labrador with 1920. Why is Newfoundland still grey?
grade4: Compare Labrador with 1920. Why is Newfoundland still grey?
grade7: Compare Labrador with 1920. Why is Newfoundland still grey? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Newfoundland joins Canada
summary: On March 31, Newfoundland enters Confederation as Canada’s tenth province. It includes the island of Newfoundland and Labrador on the mainland.
watch: Find both parts of the new province. What has changed since 1927?
grade4: Find both parts of the new province. What has changed since 1927?

title: Nunavut is created
summary: On April 1, the eastern part of the Northwest Territories becomes Nunavut. Its creation follows years of Inuit work and negotiations, including the 1993 Nunavut Land Claims Agreement. Canada now has three territories.
watch: Compare Nunavut with the remaining Northwest Territories. Why might new boundaries matter to the people living there?
grade4: Compare Nunavut with the remaining Northwest Territories. Why might new boundaries matter to the people living there?
grade7: Compare Nunavut with the remaining Northwest Territories. Why might new boundaries matter to the people living there? What political decision or agreement helps explain the change?

title: Newfoundland and Labrador
summary: On December 6, the province’s official name changes from Newfoundland to Newfoundland and Labrador. This is a name change, not a boundary change.

title: Yukon’s official name changes
summary: The new Yukon Act takes effect on April 1. The official name changes from Yukon Territory to Yukon. The territorial boundary remains the same.
